options: A law that web apps must legally comply with
A free, data-driven list of the most common and impactful web application security risks, refreshed periodically
A ranking of the most popular web frameworks
A paid security certification for developers

explain.right: It's a widely used, free list from OWASP of the most common web risks, updated every few years (current edition: 2025) — a shared checklist, not a law or cert.
explain.wrong: It isn't legislation, a certification, or a framework ranking; it's guidance drawn from real-world data.

items.q: What is the root cause of an injection vulnerability like SQL injection?
options: The user's internet connection is insecure
Untrusted input is mixed into a command or query so it's treated as code instead of data
The database is too old
The server runs too slowly to check input

explain.right: Injection happens when data and code get mixed in one string, so attacker input changes the command/query itself.
explain.wrong: It's not about speed, database age, or the user's connection — it's the code/data mixing.

items.q: What's the most reliable fix for SQL injection?
options: Use parameterized queries (placeholders) so the database always treats user values as data, never as query structure
Hide the database behind a secret port
Filter out 'bad' characters like quotes from user input
Trust input from logged-in users since they're authenticated

explain.right: Parameterized queries separate code from data structurally, so input can never change the query — the real fix.
explain.wrong: Blocklisting characters is fragile (encodings slip through), a secret port is obscurity, and authenticated users can still be malicious or compromised.

items.q: A user changes /invoice/123 to /invoice/124 in the URL and sees someone else's invoice. This is:
options: Impossible if the site uses HTTPS
Broken access control (an IDOR) — the server didn't check that the invoice belongs to this user
Fine, because the user was logged in
A problem only if the invoice contained a password

explain.right: The server must verify ownership on every object access; without it, changing an ID exposes other users' data — broken access control, #1 on the 2025 list.
explain.wrong: Being logged in isn't authorization for that specific record, any exposed data counts, and HTTPS only protects transit.

items.q: Your app 'hides' the admin page by not showing a link to it in the menu. Is that access control?
options: Yes — if users can't see the link, they can't reach it
Yes, as long as the URL is hard to guess
Only an issue for pages that change data
No — the attacker doesn't use your menu; authorization must be enforced on the server for the endpoint itself

explain.right: Hiding a UI link is not access control; the server must check 'is this user allowed?' on the endpoint, because requests can be made directly.
explain.wrong: Attackers bypass the UI and guess or discover URLs; obscurity and 'read-only' pages still leak if unprotected.
